question: Mustard crops in our village showed white rust spots, dark concentric ring lesions, and twisted flower heads this season. What diseases are these and how should farmers spray to control them?
context: Important diseases affecting rapeseed and mustard include white rust, Alternaria blight, and downy mildew. White rust causes deformation of floral parts and zig-zag branching with white fungal growth. Alternaria blight produces circular dark spots with concentric rings on leaves, especially under humid conditions. Downy mildew causes malformed and twisted inflorescences covered with white cottony growth. These diseases can be controlled by spraying mancozeb at about 1.5 kg per hectare at the initial appearance of symptoms and repeating the spray one to three times at intervals of about 15 days.

question: Mustard aphids appear every January in large colonies on flowering mustard in our district and can wipe out yield if not checked. What is the recommended spray to control mustard aphid?
context: The most serious insect pest of rapeseed and mustard is the mustard aphid. The pest sucks plant sap and reduces crop yield. Effective control can be achieved by spraying oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox 25 EC) or dimethoate (Rogor 30 EC) at about 625-1000 ml diluted in 625-1000 liters of water per hectare.

question: Mustard farmers in our cooperative harvest at different pod maturity stages and get inconsistent oil content. When should rapeseed and mustard be harvested and what yields are expected under normal conditions?
context: Rapeseed and mustard crops are harvested when about 75 percent of the pods turn yellow and the seed moisture content is around 30-40 percent. The harvested plants are bundled and dried in the sun before threshing. For safe storage, seed moisture should be reduced to below 8 percent. Under normal conditions, rapeseed yields about 1.4-2.0 tonnes per hectare, while mustard yields about 2.0-2.5 tonnes per hectare. Average yields include toria about 12-15 quintals per hectare and rai about 15-20 quintals per hectare.

question: Groundnut farmers in our cooperative in Gujarat supply to oil mills and snack food manufacturers. What makes groundnut nutritionally valuable and where does India stand in global groundnut production?
context: Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea L.), also known as peanut or mungfali, is an important oilseed crop. Groundnut seeds contain about 45 percent oil and 26 percent protein, making them highly nutritious. Peanuts are also rich in niacin, folate, fiber, magnesium, vitamin E, manganese, and phosphorus. Globally, India ranks first in area and second in production of groundnut. In India, the crop is cultivated on about 5.86 million hectares with a production of around 8.26 million tonnes and an average productivity of about 1411 kg per hectare.

question: Groundnut farmers in our sandy loam area want to know which improved varieties give the best yields in their region. Which groundnut varieties are recommended for cultivation in different parts of India?
context: Several improved groundnut varieties are recommended for cultivation in different regions. Important varieties include ICGS 76, Tirupati 2, Girnar 1, ICGS 37, ALR 3, ICGS 11, HNG 10, Punjab Mungphali 1, Mukta, Chitra, Jyoti, RS-1, M-335, MH-4, BG-2, TG-1, and TMV-6.

question: Groundnut leaves in several fields in our village showed circular brownish-black spots surrounded by yellow halos this kharif. What disease caused this damage and how should it be managed?
context: Tikka disease, also known as leaf spot disease, causes circular or irregular reddish-brown to black spots on leaves surrounded by a yellow halo. The spots appear darker on the upper surface and lighter on the lower surface of leaves. The disease can be controlled by spraying the crop two to three times with fungicides such as dithane M-45 or blitox-50 at about 1.5-2.0 kg per hectare at intervals of 10-15 days starting from the first appearance of the disease.

question: Groundnut plants in sandy soil fields of our cooperative suddenly wilted and died before the pods matured. White grub larvae were found in the soil. How should farmers treat against white grub in groundnut?
context: White grub is an important pest of groundnut. The larvae feed on soil organic matter initially and later attack plant roots and pods, causing plants to wilt and die. The pest is more common in light soils. Effective control can be achieved by treating seeds with chlorpyriphos 20 EC at about 15 ml per kg seed before sowing.

question: Groundnut farmers in our cooperative lose yield by harvesting too early or too late. How can a farmer tell when groundnut is ready to harvest and what yield should good management produce?
context: Groundnut should be harvested when the inner shell turns black and the testa color of kernels is fully developed, indicating about 80 percent pod maturity. After harvesting, pods are dried in the sun to reduce moisture to about 20-25 percent before threshing. Under normal cultivation conditions, groundnut yields about 15-25 quintals of pods per hectare with a shelling percentage of about 68-69 percent.

question: Sunflower is grown in our Andhra Pradesh district as a rabi oilseed crop after paddy harvest. What makes sunflower a good oilseed crop and what is the nutritional quality of sunflower oil?
context: Sunflower (Helianthus annuus L.), commonly known as Surajmukhi, is an important oilseed crop in India. The seeds contain about 40-43 percent high-quality edible oil. Sunflower oil is suitable for refined edible oil and vanaspati because it contains a high proportion of polyunsaturated fatty acids and has a pleasant flavour and good nutritional value. The oil also has anti-cholesterol properties and contains vitamins A, B, D, and E. Sunflower is widely cultivated because of its short duration, photo-insensitivity, and wide adaptability to different environments.

question: Sunflower growers in our cooperative want to know which hybrid varieties are best to grow in their region for maximum oil yield.
context: Several improved sunflower varieties and hybrids have been developed for higher productivity and better adaptability. Important varieties include CO-5, TAS-82, DRSF-113, DRSF-108, TNAU SUF-7, and GAU SUF-15. Popular hybrids include KBSH-41, KBSH-42, NDSH-1, RSFH-1, APSH-11, Suryamukhi, BSH-1, MSFH-1, MSFH-8, MSFH-17, LSH-1, LSH-3, and PSFH-67.

question: Sunflower seedlings in our cooperative fields where potatoes were grown previously were cut at the base by a pest in large numbers in March. What pest caused this and how can it be controlled?
context: Cutworms are important insect pests of sunflower, especially during March-April in fields where sunflower follows potato. The caterpillars cut the seedlings at ground level causing serious damage. The pest can be controlled by applying chlorpyriphos at about 5 liters per hectare mixed with 10 kg fine soil and broadcasting it uniformly in the field before sowing after the last ploughing.

question: Sunflower farmers in our FPO are not sure at what stage to harvest the heads and what oil content to expect. When should sunflower be harvested and what grain yield can well-managed sunflower fields produce?
context: Sunflower is ready for harvest when the back of the flower head turns yellowish-brown and the seed moisture content is about 20 percent. The harvested heads are dried in the sun before threshing. Under good crop management practices, sunflower yields about 2 tonnes of grain per hectare.

question: Cotton farmers in our Vidarbha region grow both desi and Bt hybrids. What makes cotton such a valuable commercial crop and why is it called white gold in India?
context: Cotton (Gossypium spp.) is one of the most important commercial crops in India and is commonly referred to as white gold because of its great economic value. It is primarily cultivated for fibre used in the textile industry, while cotton seeds are used to produce cottonseed oil, which is used as cooking oil. India has the largest cotton acreage in the world with about 11.99 million hectares and a production of around 6 million tonnes with an average yield of about 512 kg per hectare.

question: Cotton farmers in our cooperative growing Bt hybrids want to know how much seed is needed and what is the recommended spacing for different types of cotton varieties.
context: Seed rate in cotton varies depending on species, hybrids, and cultivation conditions. For American cotton Bt hybrids about 0.75 kg seed per acre is used, while non-Bt hybrid varieties require about 1.5 kg per acre. Desi cotton hybrids require about 1.25 kg per acre, while desi cotton varieties require about 3 kg per acre. Cotton is usually sown between the first week of April and mid-May. Seeds are sown in rows spaced about 67.5 cm apart using a cotton sowing drill, and plants are maintained at spacing of about 45-60 cm within rows.

question: Cotton plants in our district suddenly wilted and died without any leaf yellowing in patches across the field. Root rot fungus was suspected. What diseases cause wilting in cotton and how should they be treated?
context: Important diseases affecting cotton include root rot and Fusarium wilt. Root rot causes sudden wilting and death of plants without visible discoloration of leaves. It can be controlled by drenching the soil with carbendazim at about 0.2 percent concentration. Fusarium wilt causes stunting, yellowing, wilting, and leaf drop in both young and mature plants. The disease can be controlled by soaking cotton seeds in water containing bavistin before sowing.

question: Pink bollworm is the most feared pest for cotton farmers in our district. What is pink bollworm and do Bt cotton varieties protect against it?
context: Pink bollworm is one of the most destructive pests of cotton in many cotton-growing regions. The pest damages cotton bolls and reduces yield. Bt cotton varieties provide effective protection against major bollworm pests including pink bollworm.

question: Cotton farmers in our cooperative need to know how much water to apply and at which crop growth stages irrigation is most critical to prevent boll shedding.
context: Cotton generally requires about four to six irrigations depending on rainfall and soil conditions. The first irrigation is usually given about 4-6 weeks after sowing, and subsequent irrigations are applied at intervals of about two to three weeks. Sowing cotton on ridges and irrigating through furrows helps save irrigation water. Critical irrigation stages include the beginning of sympodial branching at about 60-70 days after sowing, flowering at 90-100 days, boll formation at around 125 days, and boll bursting at around 140 days.

question: Cotton growers in our cooperative do their picking in batches as bolls open. How many pickings are needed and what yield can hybrid cotton fields produce per hectare?
context: Cotton is harvested manually in about three to four pickings as the bolls mature. Under improved cultivation practices, cotton yields about 1.5-2 tonnes of seed cotton (kapas) per hectare, and even higher yields can be obtained from hybrid cotton varieties. About 33 percent of kapas is cotton lint and about 66 percent is cotton seed.

question: Sugarcane farmers in our UP cooperative supply cane to the local sugar mill. What species of sugarcane are grown commercially and what special characteristic makes sugarcane a C4 plant?
context: Sugarcane belongs to the genus Saccharum, which includes five important species. Saccharum officinarum is highly valued because of its high sucrose content. Sugarcane is a tall perennial plant that can grow up to 5-6 meters and produces multiple stems. It is a C4 plant with high efficiency in storing solar energy and converting it into sucrose. Brazil is the largest producer of sugarcane in the world followed by India.

question: Sugarcane growers in our cooperative complain that water use in sugarcane is too high. How much water does sugarcane need throughout the growing season and what are the recommended efficient irrigation methods?
context: Sugarcane requires large amounts of water. In tropical regions irrigation is usually given every 7 days during germination, every 10 days during tillering, every 7 days during the grand growth phase, and every 15 days during maturity depending on rainfall. About 30-40 irrigations may be required in tropical areas, while in subtropical regions about 7-10 irrigations are generally sufficient. Approximately 250 tonnes of water are required to produce one tonne of sugarcane. Efficient irrigation methods such as alternate furrow irrigation, drip irrigation, and trash mulching help conserve water.

question: Sugarcane fields in our cooperative are heavily infested with weeds early in the season before the crop canopy closes. What are the recommended herbicides for weed control in sugarcane fields?
context: For weed control in sugarcane, pre-emergence herbicides such as atrazine at about 2 kg per hectare or oxyfluorfen at about 750 ml per hectare mixed in 500 liters of water are applied on the third day after planting in pure sugarcane crops. Under intercropping systems with soybean, blackgram, or groundnut, pre-emergence application of thiobencarb at about 1.25 kg active ingredient per hectare provides effective weed control.

question: Sugarcane farmers in our cooperative district want to know when to harvest for maximum sugar recovery and what total yield is achievable under good management.
context: Sugarcane is harvested after reaching maturity. In subtropical regions harvesting usually begins in October and continues until May, whereas in tropical regions harvesting generally begins in December and continues until May. With good management practices sugarcane yields about 120-150 tonnes per hectare depending on the growing period and whether it is a plant crop or ratoon crop. The average sugar recovery in India is about 10.25 percent.

question: Coffee planters in our Karnataka cooperative grow both arabica and robusta varieties at different elevations. What climate conditions does each species of coffee need to grow well?
context: Coffea arabica is usually grown at elevations between 1000 and 1500 meters and requires annual rainfall of about 1600-2500 mm. Coffea robusta grows at lower elevations of about 500-1000 meters. Coffee plants require deep, friable soils rich in organic matter with a pH of about 6.0-6.5. Planting pits of about 45 x 45 x 45 cm are prepared and filled with top soil mixed with farmyard manure or compost.

question: Tea estate workers in Assam ask about the correct plucking schedule to maintain quality and yield. How should tea leaves be harvested and how frequently should plucking be done?
context: Tea leaves are harvested by plucking young shoots consisting of two or three leaves and a bud. Plucking is usually done every 7-10 days during peak production periods and every 12-15 days during slower growth periods. Proper plucking ensures good quality tea leaves.

question: Tea growers in our cooperative say their plantations need special management operations beyond just plucking. What are the important cultural operations specific to tea plantation management?
context: Tea cultivation involves several specialized operations including training, centering, tipping, plucking, shade management, pollarding, and annual lopping. These operations help maintain plant structure, improve branching, and increase the number of plucking points for higher yields.

question: Jute growers in our West Bengal cooperative sell their fibre to sacking and rope manufacturers. What is jute and what types are grown commercially in India?
context: Jute (Corchorus spp.) is an important natural fibre crop. The two major cultivated species are white jute (Corchorus capsularis) and Tossa jute (Corchorus olitorius). Jute fibre is widely used to produce products such as Hessian cloth, gunny bags, ropes, and carpets. It is one of the most affordable natural fibres. In India, jute production is mainly concentrated in Assam, Odisha, Bihar, and West Bengal.

question: Jute farmers in our district struggle with high labour costs for weeding after sowing. What chemical weed control methods are effective in jute fields?
context: Weed management includes two hand weedings at about 20-25 days and 35-40 days after sowing. Chemical weed control can be done by applying pendimethalin at about 1 kg active ingredient per hectare as a pre-emergence herbicide. Post-emergence herbicides such as fenoxaprop-ethyl or quizalofop-ethyl applied around 21 days after sowing can effectively control grassy weeds.

question: Jute growers in our cooperative need to know the right time to cut jute and what fibre yield they can expect from well-managed fields.
context: Jute is generally harvested between about 100 and 110 days after sowing. After harvesting, plants are left in the field for 3-4 days for leaf shedding. Plants are then bundled and processed for fibre extraction. The average green plant yield is about 45-50 tonnes per hectare and fibre yield is about 2.0-2.5 tonnes per hectare.

question: After jute harvest, farmers in our district ret the stems in ponds and waterways to extract fibre. What is the retting process and which method gives the best quality fibre?
context: Retting is the process of separating jute fibre from the plant stem. Several retting methods exist including mechanical retting, chemical retting, steam or dew retting, and water or microbial retting. Among these, water or microbial retting is the most common traditional method used to extract fine bast fibres from jute stems.

question: Apple growers in our Himachal Pradesh cooperative want to establish new orchards with better planting systems. What planting systems and spacings are recommended for apple orchards in hilly areas?
context: In flat areas, apple trees are planted using square, rectangular, quincunx or hexagonal planting systems, whereas in hilly areas contour or terrace planting is preferred. In India, a spacing of 8 x 8 meters is recommended for vigorous cultivars and 5 x 5 meters for dwarf varieties. Pits of 1 x 1 x 1 meter are prepared and filled with a mixture of top soil, 40-50 kg farmyard manure, 500 g superphosphate and insecticidal dust before planting.

question: Apple orchards in our cooperative are producing poor fruit set even though trees flower well. What causes poor fruit set in apple trees and how do orchard managers solve this problem?
context: Most apple cultivars, especially those belonging to the Delicious group, are self-infertile and therefore require cross pollination for satisfactory fruit set. Pollinizer varieties such as Tydeman's Early Worcester, Red Gold and Golden Delicious are planted along with the main commercial varieties to ensure proper pollination.

question: Apple orchardists in our area apply fertilizers at random times without a proper schedule. What fertilizer doses and timing are recommended for apple trees at different ages?
context: Generally, one-year-old apple plants require about 10 kg farmyard manure, 70 g nitrogen, 35 g phosphorus (P2O5) and 70 g potassium (K2O). Farmyard manure, phosphorus and potassium are applied during winter before snowfall, while nitrogen is applied about one month before bud break.

question: Apple growers in our cooperative harvest fruits at different stages and face problems with shelf life and storage. What maturity signs should be checked before harvesting apple and how long can apples be stored?
context: Apples should be harvested at the correct stage of maturity. Important maturity indices include browning of seeds, change in ground colour from green to pale or red, TSS of about 11-14.5 percent, and easy separation of fruit from the spur. Apples can be stored at temperatures between -1.1 degrees C and 0 degrees C with 85-90 percent relative humidity for about 4-6 months.

question: Mango orchards are the main source of income for fruit farmers in our district. What nutrients does mango provide and why is it called the national fruit of India?
context: Mango (Mangifera indica L.) is popularly known as the king of fruits and is considered the national fruit of India. Mango is an excellent source of vitamin A, a good source of vitamin C, and contains several important minerals and nutrients.

question: Mango growers in our UP belt want to know which variety to plant depending on whether they are in north or south India. Which commercial mango varieties are grown in different regions of India?
context: Important commercial mango varieties include Dashehari, Langra, Chausa and Bombay Green in northern India; Banganpalli, Neelum and Totapuri in southern India; Alphonso and Kesar in western India; and Langra and Himsagar in eastern India.

question: Mango orchardists in our cooperative use stone grafting and veneer grafting to multiply their best trees. How are mango plants propagated for commercial orchards?
context: Mango can be propagated by both sexual and asexual methods. However, commercial orchards are mainly established using vegetative propagation methods such as veneer grafting, stone grafting and softwood grafting.

question: Mango orchards in our district suffer from leaf hopper, mealy bug, and powdery mildew every year. What are the major pests and diseases affecting mango and how are they controlled?
context: Important pests of mango include mango leaf hopper, mango mealy bug, stone weevil and fruit fly. Major diseases include powdery mildew and anthracnose. These problems are controlled using appropriate insecticides, fungicides and sanitation practices.

question: Alphonso mango growers in our cooperative export fruits to the Gulf but face rejection due to spongy tissue inside the fruit. What is spongy tissue disorder in mango and what causes it?
context: Spongy tissue disorder, common in Alphonso mango, causes a sour and spongy patch inside the fruit pulp making it unfit for consumption.

question: Banana farmers in our Kerala cooperative grow several varieties for both local markets and processing into chips. What soil and climate conditions are needed for good banana cultivation?
context: Banana grows well in clay to sandy clay loam soils, with medium textured soils considered ideal. The suitable soil pH ranges from about 5.5 to 8.0. Banana grows best in areas with temperatures between about 21 degrees C and 32 degrees C and annual rainfall ranging from about 1000 to 2000 mm.

question: Banana growers in our area allow too many suckers to grow and end up with a crowded poorly productive clump. What is desuckering in banana farming and how should sucker management be done?
context: Desuckering refers to the removal of unwanted suckers from the banana clump. Generally one bearing plant, one follower and one sucker are maintained in each clump while the remaining weak suckers are removed.

question: Banana plantations in our cooperative face serious losses from Fusarium wilt and bunchy top virus every year. What are the major diseases and pests of banana and how should they be managed?
context: Important pests include corm weevil, stem borer and nematodes. Major diseases include leaf spot, Panama disease (Fusarium wilt) and bunchy top virus. Control measures include use of disease-free planting material, sanitation practices and application of suitable pesticides or fungicides.

question: Guava orchardists in our UP district earn good income from Allahabad Safeda and Sardar varieties. What are the best varieties of guava and which states produce the most guava in India?
context: Important guava varieties include Allahabad Safeda, Sardar (Lucknow-49), Behat Coconut, Seedless, Apple Colour, Banarasi Surkha, Chittidar, Arka Kiran and Swetha. Major guava producing states in India include Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Maharashtra.

question: Guava growers in our cooperative want to regulate their trees to produce only the winter crop for better fruit quality and price. What is crop regulation in guava and how is it practiced?
context: Guava may flower two or three times a year depending on the region. Crop regulation is practiced to obtain high-quality fruits, usually by avoiding the rainy season crop and promoting winter crop through pruning, root exposure, or chemical sprays such as NAA or 2,4-D.

question: Guava orchards in our cooperative suffer badly from fruit fly and guava wilt which reduces the lifespan of trees. What are the major pests and diseases in guava orchards and how can they be controlled?
context: Important pests include fruit fly and mealy bug which damage fruits and shoots. Major diseases include guava wilt and anthracnose. Management practices include sanitation, destruction of infected fruits, use of resistant varieties and spraying recommended fungicides or insecticides.

question: Guava orchardists in our area want to know when to harvest for the best sweetness and how much yield a mature grafted guava tree gives.
context: Guava fruits are harvested when their colour changes from green to yellowish. Seedling plants start bearing after about 5-6 years, whereas grafted plants begin bearing after about 2-3 years. An 8-10 year old guava tree can yield about 400-800 fruits weighing around 80-100 kg.

question: Sweet orange and mandarin farmers in our Nagpur cooperative sell to juice factories and local markets. What are all the different crops included under citrus cultivation in India?
context: Citrus fruits include mandarin (Citrus reticulata), sweet orange (Citrus sinensis), lemon (Citrus limon), lime (Citrus aurantifolia), pummelo (Citrus grandis) and grapefruit (Citrus paradisi). The edible portion of citrus fruits is the juice present in the vesicles, which contains about 12-14 percent sugars along with citric acid and vitamin C (ascorbic acid). In India, major citrus producing states include Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, the North-Eastern states, Karnataka and Bihar.

question: Citrus growers in our cooperative grafted on rough lemon rootstocks are having gummosis problems. Which rootstocks are recommended for citrus and why does rootstock choice matter?
context: Common rootstocks used for citrus include rough lemon, sour orange, Karna Khatta, Rangpur lime, sweet orange, citranges such as Troyer, trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) and Cleopatra mandarin.

question: Mosambi oranges in our cooperative are turning dry and granular inside even though the outside looks normal. What is causing this physiological disorder and how can it be prevented?
context: Granulation and fruit cracking are common disorders in citrus fruits. Granulation causes juice sacs to become hard, colourless and tasteless, particularly in varieties like Mosambi. Fruit cracking is often caused by irregular irrigation and environmental stress. These problems can be reduced through proper irrigation and application of growth regulators or micronutrients.

question: Citrus orchards in our region face aphid attacks, citrus canker, and gummosis every season. What are the major pests and diseases of citrus orchards and how should they be managed?
context: Major pests include aphids, citrus psylla, leaf miner, lemon butterfly and fruit sucking moth. Important diseases include tristeza, citrus greening, phytophthora rot (gummosis) and bacterial canker. These problems can be managed through sanitation practices, use of resistant rootstocks and application of appropriate insecticides and fungicides.

question: Grape vineyards in our Maharashtra cooperative grow Thompson Seedless for raisin making and fresh market. What climate and soil conditions does grapevine cultivation need to produce good quality fruit?
context: Grapes grow best in well-drained sandy loam soils rich in organic matter. Heavy clay soils, sands or silts are unsuitable. The crop requires a long, dry and moderately hot season for berry ripening followed by cool winter conditions. Bright sunny days help in sugar accumulation in berries.

question: Grape growers in our cooperative use bower and trellis systems for training but are confused about which system suits which variety. How should grapevines be trained and pruned for good production?
context: Training is done to shape the vine and improve fruit production. Common systems include head, trellis, kniffin and bower systems. The bower or pergola system is most widely used for vigorous varieties. Pruning is done to regulate crop load and maintain vine health.

question: Grape vineyards in our cooperative face powdery mildew and downy mildew every year that ruins the berry quality. What are the major diseases affecting grapevines and what fungicides are used to control them?
context: Important pests include chafer beetles and thrips which damage leaves and buds. Major diseases include powdery mildew, downy mildew and anthracnose. These diseases are controlled by spraying fungicides such as wettable sulphur, Bordeaux mixture and copper oxychloride.

question: Grape farmers in our cooperative want to improve berry size and bunch looseness to fetch better market prices. What crop regulation techniques improve the quality of grapes?
context: Crop regulation techniques include pruning, thinning of clusters and berries, girdling and application of growth regulators such as GA3. These practices help improve berry size, bunch looseness, ripening and fruit quality.

question: Potato farmers in our UP district supply to chips factories and local vegetable markets. What makes potato such an important food crop and what nutrients does it provide?
context: Potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) belongs to the family Solanaceae and is one of the most important food crops in the world. It is a major source of starch and is rich in carbohydrates, vitamins such as B1, B2, B6 and C, and minerals like calcium, phosphorus and iron.

question: Potato growers in our cooperative want to know which varieties to use for processing into chips versus which ones are best for fresh market sales.
context: Potato varieties include early varieties such as Kufri Ashoka, Kufri Chandermukhi, Kufri Jawahar and Kufri Lauvkar; main season varieties like Kufri Jyoti, Kufri Sutlej and Kufri Pukhraj; late varieties such as Kufri Jeevan and Kufri Naveen; and processing varieties like Kufri Chipsona 1, Kufri Chipsona 2 and Kufri Chipsona 3.

question: Potato leaves in several fields of our cooperative showed brownish-black water-soaked lesions rapidly spreading and rotting the tubers. What diseases caused this and how should they be managed?
context: Important diseases include early blight and late blight. Early blight causes brown concentric spots on leaves while late blight produces water soaked lesions and rotting of tubers.

question: Potato growers in our district want to know when the crop is ready to dig and what yield is expected from early and late maturing varieties.
context: Potatoes are harvested when the crop matures and the haulms turn yellow. Early varieties yield about 200 quintals per hectare while late varieties may yield about 300 quintals per hectare.

question: Cauliflower farmers in our cooperative grow three different batches from August to January. What climate and soil conditions are needed for cauliflower cultivation and how are varieties classified?
context: Cauliflower grows well in fertile soils with good water holding capacity and a pH range of about 6.0 to 6.5. Temperature plays an important role during curd formation and development. Cauliflower varieties are classified based on maturity period such as early varieties, mid-early varieties, mid-late varieties and late snowball types depending on their temperature requirement for curd formation.

question: Cauliflower growers in our block frequently see problems like buttonheads, ricey curds, and blind plants. What physiological disorders affect cauliflower curd development and what causes them?
context: Important physiological disorders include buttoning, riceyness, blindness and whip tail, which affect curd development and crop quality.

question: Cabbage and cauliflower farmers in our cooperative face diamondback moth and aphids every season. What are the major diseases and insect pests attacking cabbage crops?
context: Important diseases include black leg, downy mildew, black rot and bacterial soft rot which damage leaves and roots of cabbage plants. Major insect pests include diamondback moth, aphids and cabbage butterfly which damage leaves and heads by feeding on plant tissues.

question: Okra is grown across our district in both summer and kharif seasons. Which improved varieties are recommended and what seed rate and spacing should be followed for okra cultivation?
context: Important varieties include Parbhani Kranti, Punjab Padmani, Arka Anamika, Arka Abhay, Pusa Makhmali, Pusa A-4 and Pusa Sawani. Seed rate is about 15-20 kg per hectare for spring-summer crops and 10-12 kg per hectare for rainy season crops. Spacing is about 30-45 cm between rows and 15 cm between plants.

question: Okra fields in our cooperative show yellow vein mosaic symptoms and fruit borer damage every kharif season. What are the major diseases and pests attacking okra and how are they managed?
context: Major diseases include powdery mildew and yellow vein mosaic disease which affect leaves and reduce yield. Important pests include fruit borer and whitefly which damage shoots and fruits and also transmit viral diseases.

question: Cumin is the most important spice crop for farmers in our Rajasthan district where it fetches good export prices. What makes cumin a valuable spice and what are the improved varieties farmers should grow?
context: Cumin (Cuminum cyminum), also called Safaid jeera, belongs to the family Apiaceae and is one of the oldest spices known to mankind. The seeds are yellowish to greyish-brown with a characteristic aromatic odour due to the compound cuminol and have a spicy, slightly bitter taste. They are widely used as a condiment in food. Important cumin varieties grown in India include RS-1, Gujarat Cumin-1, MC-43 and Vijapur-5.

question: Cumin crops in our district suffer heavy losses from aphid attack and Fusarium wilt every season. What are the major pests and diseases of cumin and how should farmers control them?
context: Aphids are common insect pests of cumin and can be controlled by spraying insecticides like phosphomidon or dimethoate. A serious disease of cumin is wilt caused by Fusarium species, which can be reduced using organic amendments such as neem cake.

question: Cumin farmers in our cooperative want to know when to harvest to avoid seed loss and what average yield they can expect.
context: Cumin crop matures in about 80-120 days after sowing. Plants are uprooted when the leaves turn yellow and harvested before the seeds shatter. Average yield ranges from about 8 to 15 quintals of seeds per hectare.

question: Black pepper growers in our Kerala cooperative say their vines are dying from quick wilt disease. What is black pepper, why is it called king of spices, and what diseases are the most serious threats?
context: Black pepper (Piper nigrum) belongs to the family Piperaceae and is one of the most important spice crops in the world. It is often called the King of Spices and Black Gold because of its high economic value and major contribution to foreign exchange. The pungency of pepper is due to the alkaloid piperine. An important pest is the pollu beetle which damages berries. A serious disease is quick wilt which causes leaf rot, collar rot and root rot in pepper vines.

question: Turmeric growers in our Andhra Pradesh cooperative process rhizomes into dried powder. What are the popular turmeric varieties, how much fertilizer does turmeric need, and when should it be harvested?
context: Important turmeric varieties include Kasturi, Balaga, Mundaga, Aleppey and Mannuthy Local. Farmyard manure at about 40 tonnes per hectare is applied during land preparation. Fertilizers are applied at about 30:30:60 or 60:30:90 kg NPK per hectare depending on the crop requirement. Turmeric is harvested about 7-10 months after planting. The average yield of raw turmeric rhizomes is about 20-25 tonnes per hectare.

question: Coriander farmers in our Rajasthan district grow both seed crop and green coriander. What seed rate should be used for each purpose and what fertilizer is recommended for coriander cultivation?
context: Coriander is propagated through seeds. Before sowing, the fruits are rubbed to separate the two halves. The seed rate is about 10-15 kg per hectare for irrigated crops and 25-30 kg per hectare for rainfed crops. A fertilizer dose of about 40:40:40 kg of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium per hectare is generally applied at the time of sowing.

question: Fenugreek is grown widely across our cooperative both for seeds and for green leaves. What varieties are recommended and what fertilizer dose gives good yield in fenugreek cultivation?
context: Important fenugreek varieties include Pusa Early Bunching, Pusa Early Prolific, Pusa Early Green, Pusa Early Dwarf, Pusa Early Round, Pusa Early Long, Pusa Early Thick Leaf and Pusa Early Green Leaf. The recommended seed rate is about 20-25 kg per hectare for irrigated crops and about 30-40 kg per hectare for rainfed crops. A fertilizer dose of about 20:40:20 kg NPK per hectare is generally applied at the time of sowing along with farmyard manure.

question: Dairy farmers in our cooperative raise crossbred cows and buffaloes and want to understand nutritional requirements better. What nutrients do farm animals need for good health and high production?
context: The essential nutrients required by livestock include water, energy, protein, minerals and vitamins. These nutrients are necessary for maintaining body weight, growth, reproduction, lactation and overall health of the animals.

question: Water shortages in summer affect livestock productivity badly on farms in our district. Why is water considered so critical for livestock and how much do different farm animals need daily?
context: Water is the most abundant and essential nutrient required for livestock production. Adequate supply of clean water ensures proper feed intake, digestion and body functions. Lactating cows require about 15-35 gallons of water per day, while non-lactating cows require about 15 gallons. Horses may drink up to 15 gallons daily, sheep about 1.5-3 gallons, pigs about 3-5 gallons and hens about one pint per day.

question: Cattle on farms in our block lose weight during summer when fodder is scarce. What role does protein play in livestock nutrition and what happens when animals don't get enough?
context: Protein is essential for growth, tissue repair and production. Ruminant animals can convert low quality protein into high quality protein through microbial action in the rumen. Protein deficiency leads to breakdown of body tissues and severe weight loss.

question: Livestock farmers in our cooperative practice selective breeding to improve their cattle and goat herds. What is the purpose of breeding in farm animals and how does it improve livestock?
context: Breeding refers to the process of mating selected males and females to produce offspring with desirable characteristics. It helps improve livestock quality, productivity and genetic traits.

question: Cattle breeders in our district sometimes mate closely related animals to fix good traits. What are the advantages and disadvantages of inbreeding in livestock herds?
context: Inbreeding increases homozygosity and helps fix desirable traits in a population. It also helps eliminate harmful genes by exposing lethal or semi-lethal genes in homozygous form. However, inbreeding can cause loss of genetic variability, reduced hybrid vigour, lower birth weight, poor growth, reproductive problems and increased susceptibility to diseases.

question: Livestock farmers in our cooperative introduced new unrelated bulls to improve the herd and noticed better growth and fertility in calves. What is outbreeding and what benefits does it bring to livestock herds?
context: Outbreeding is the mating of unrelated individuals. It increases heterozygosity and improves genetic variation within a population. Outbreeding produces hybrid vigour which leads to better growth, higher productivity, improved disease resistance and lower mortality rates.

question: Meat processors in our district waste large quantities of blood, bones, and organ meats from slaughter. How can livestock byproducts be utilized to generate more income from the same animals?
context: Common byproducts include blood, hides and skins, bones, organs, fats, glands and other tissues produced during slaughtering and meat processing. Livestock byproducts are used to produce animal feed, biodiesel, cosmetics, pharmaceutical products, fertilizers, collagen and biogas. Efficient utilization of byproducts increases the value of carcasses, reduces disposal costs and improves profitability of livestock and meat processing industries.

question: Seed dealers in our block sell many different grades and classes of seed. What makes a seed a quality seed and what characteristics should every farmer look for when buying seed?
context: Quality seed refers to seed that possesses all the desirable characteristics of an improved variety, including genetic purity, physical purity, high germination, good vigour, viability and proper moisture content.

question: Farmers in our FPO sometimes unknowingly buy seed mixed with seeds of other varieties or weed seeds. What is genetic purity and physical purity in seeds and why do they matter?
context: Genetic purity refers to the percentage of contamination by seeds or genetic material of other varieties or species. For example, breeder seed has about 100 percent genetic purity, foundation seed about 99 percent and certified seed about 98 percent. Physical purity is the proportion of pure seed in a seed lot along with the absence of other crop seeds, weed seeds and inert materials. For most crops, physical purity should be about 98 percent.

question: Seed stored in our cooperative warehouse failed to germinate when farmers sowed it next season. What determines seed germination percentage and why is it important for crop establishment?
context: Germination percentage refers to the proportion of seeds in a lot that are capable of developing into normal seedlings under suitable conditions, according to the standards of the Indian Minimum Seed Certification Standards.

question: Some farmers in our FPO complain that even when germination percentage is high, seedling emergence in the field is very poor and uneven. What is seed vigour and how is it different from germination percentage?
context: Seed vigour refers to the sum of seed properties that determine the potential for rapid, uniform emergence and development of seedlings under a wide range of field conditions.

question: Farmers storing seed grain at home often find it fails to germinate the next season. What moisture level should be maintained for safe storage of different types of crop seeds?
context: Moisture content refers to the amount of water present in the seed. For example, cereals require about 10-12 percent moisture, pulses 7-9 percent, oilseeds 6-7 percent and vegetables about 5-6 percent for safe storage.

question: Seed companies in our district supply certified, foundation, and breeder seed. What are the different stages of seed multiplication and how does seed move from breeder to farmer?
context: Seed multiplication occurs in four stages: nucleus seed, breeder seed, foundation seed and certified seed. Nucleus seed is the original seed of an improved variety maintained by the plant breeder. Breeder seed is produced from nucleus seed and is identified with a golden yellow tag. Foundation seed is produced from breeder seed and is identified with a white tag. Certified seed is produced from foundation seed and distributed to farmers for commercial crop production, identified with a blue tag.

question: Seed growers in our cooperative want to know what isolation distance to maintain between seed crop plots to prevent cross contamination. What is isolation in seed production and why is it necessary?
context: Isolation is the separation of seed crops from other crops to prevent contamination and cross-pollination. It can be achieved through time isolation or space isolation.

question: Seed crop farmers in our block need to understand what roguing is and why it is important for maintaining variety purity in seed plots.
context: Roughing is the removal of off-type plants or plants that differ from the true characteristics of the variety during seed production.

question: Maize and sorghum farmers in our area want to know why hybrid seeds give better yield than variety seeds and what is the basis for hybrid superiority.
context: A hybrid is the offspring produced by crossing two genetically different parents to combine desirable characteristics from both. An inbred line is a plant line produced through continuous self-pollination in cross-pollinated crops and is often used as a parental line for hybrid seed production.

question: Soil erosion is a serious problem in our hilly district where runoff carries away the topsoil every monsoon. Why is protecting soil and water so important for sustainable farming?
context: Soil and water are valuable natural resources that must be conserved for sustainable agriculture and future generations. About 50 percent of cultivated land in India suffers from soil erosion, making conservation practices essential to maintain soil fertility and crop productivity.

question: After heavy rains, farmers in our area see a lot of water running off their fields carrying fine soil particles. What is runoff and how does it cause soil erosion and loss of nutrients?
context: Runoff is the portion of rainfall or irrigation water that flows away from the field either on the surface or below the surface instead of being absorbed by the soil. Unmanaged runoff is a major cause of soil erosion.

question: Trees and grasses on bunds in our cooperative fields seem to reduce soil erosion and water loss. How does vegetation help reduce runoff and protect soil on farm land?
context: Vegetation reduces soil erosion by intercepting rainfall, slowing down runoff, binding soil particles through roots, increasing soil organic matter, improving soil structure and enhancing water infiltration and storage capacity.

question: After rain, a thin layer of soil seems to wash away from fields in our village even though there are no visible channels or gullies. What type of erosion is this and why is it a concern for farmers?
context: Sheet erosion is the uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil by rainfall and surface runoff. It usually occurs slowly on gentle slopes and often goes unnoticed by farmers.

question: Farmers in our cooperative noticed small shallow channels forming on their fields after heavy rain. They can still plough them out. What type of erosion is this?
context: Rill erosion occurs when runoff water forms small shallow channels or rills in the soil surface. These channels can be removed through normal cultivation practices.

question: Deep channels that cannot be filled by ploughing have formed in some fields in our district after years of uncontrolled water flow. What type of severe erosion is this?
context: Gully erosion is an advanced stage of soil erosion where deep channels or gullies are formed due to continuous water flow. These cannot be easily corrected by normal cultivation.

question: Strong dusty winds in our arid district carry away fine soil particles from bare fallow fields every summer. What type of erosion is this and how serious is it for farming land?
context: Wind erosion is the movement of soil particles caused by strong wind forces that lift or drag soil particles across the land surface.

question: Farmers in our FPO want to adopt conservation farming practices to stop soil loss. What are the most important soil conservation measures that can be practiced on farms?
context: Important soil conservation measures include conservation tillage, minimum tillage, zero tillage, strip cropping, crop rotation, mulching, land leveling, proper drainage and growing vegetation on bunds.

question: Zero tillage wheat cultivation is spreading in our district after farmers saw higher profits and better soil health from it. What is zero tillage and what specific advantages does it offer compared to conventional tillage?
context: Zero tillage is a farming practice where crops are planted directly into the soil without ploughing, except for opening a narrow slot for seed placement. Zero tillage helps reduce soil erosion, conserve soil moisture, improve nitrogen availability, protect seedlings, reduce labour and fuel costs and maintain crop yields comparable to traditional tillage systems.

question: Farmers in our cooperative on sloping fields grow wheat and mustard in alternating strips to reduce erosion. What is strip cropping and how does it protect soil on sloping land?
context: Strip cropping is the practice of growing different crops in alternating strips along the slope to reduce soil erosion and improve soil conservation.

question: Rice straw and dry crop residues are used as mulch on vegetable beds in our cooperative. What is mulching and what benefits does it provide to the soil and crops?
context: Mulching is the practice of covering the soil surface with crop residues or organic materials to conserve moisture, reduce erosion and improve soil fertility.

question: Water scarcity is the biggest challenge for farmers in our semi-arid district. What is irrigation in farming and what factors should be considered before deciding on an irrigation method?
context: Irrigation is the artificial supply of water to crops when rainfall is insufficient to meet the water requirements for plant growth and development. Important factors include land slope, soil type, effective rainfall, crop water requirement, irrigation method and quality of irrigation water.

question: Rice farmers in our delta area use basin irrigation with earthen bunds around each plot. What is basin irrigation and for which crops and conditions is it most suitable?
context: Basin irrigation is a method where water is applied to flat areas surrounded by bunds that prevent water from flowing out of the basin. It is commonly used for crops like rice and fruit trees. Basin irrigation helps conserve rainfall, reduce soil erosion, improve water distribution efficiency and is suitable for close growing crops, orchards and many field crops.

question: Sugarcane and vegetable farmers in our cooperative use furrow irrigation to water their crops between ridges. What is furrow irrigation and for which crops does it work best?
context: Furrow irrigation is a method where water flows through small channels or furrows between crop rows, allowing water to infiltrate into the soil while crops grow on the ridges. Furrow irrigation is suitable for row crops such as maize, sunflower, sugarcane, soybean, vegetables, potatoes, beans and fruit crops like citrus and grapes. It works well on gentle slopes and helps save irrigation water through alternate or skip furrow irrigation.

question: Some progressive farmers in our block installed sprinkler systems and say they save water and labor. What is sprinkler irrigation and what benefits does it offer over surface irrigation methods?
context: Sprinkler irrigation is a method where water is pumped through pipes and sprayed into the air through sprinklers so that it falls on crops like rainfall. Sprinkler irrigation helps conserve water and soil, improves irrigation efficiency, saves labour, promotes uniform germination, supports fertigation and protects crops from frost.

question: Drip irrigation is being promoted in our district for horticultural crops. What is drip irrigation, what are the components of a drip system, and what benefits does it give to fruit and vegetable growers?
context: Drip irrigation is a method where water is applied slowly and directly to the root zone of plants through pipes and emitters at frequent intervals. A drip irrigation system consists of a pump unit, control unit, filtering unit, mainlines and sub-mainlines, laterals and emitters. Drip irrigation saves water, increases crop yield, improves water use efficiency and delivers water directly to plant roots, reducing evaporation and runoff.

question: Paddy growers in our delta region who shifted from transplanting to direct seeding want to know what the different sowing methods are for dry cultivation and how much seed each method needs.
context: In dry and semi-dry rice cultivation, farmers commonly use three sowing methods: broadcasting, drilling, and dibbling. Broadcasting involves scattering seeds over the soil surface, drilling involves placing seeds in rows using a seed drill or behind a country plough, and dibbling involves placing seeds manually into holes in the soil. For drilling, a seed rate of about 30-50 kg per hectare is used, while broadcasting requires about 60-100 kg per hectare. A row spacing of about 15-20 cm is considered optimal for upland rice cultivation.

question: Rice farmers in our cooperative struggle with a shortage of irrigation water. What is aerobic rice cultivation and how does it differ from conventional flooded paddy farming?
context: Aerobic rice cultivation involves growing high-yielding rice varieties in non-puddled and well-drained soils under irrigated conditions. Unlike traditional flooded rice fields, aerobic rice is grown in soils that remain mostly aerobic, with irrigation applied only when the soil becomes dry. This method helps save water while still achieving good yields, although proper weed management and efficient water management are critical for success.

question: Paddy growers in our cooperative use flooding and puddling as the traditional method of cultivation. How is conventional wet rice cultivation practiced and what are the key steps in this system?
context: Conventional rice cultivation is a wet cultivation system in which fields are flooded with water and the soil is puddled through repeated ploughing under standing water of about 5-7 cm depth. After puddling, rice seedlings grown in a nursery are transplanted into the prepared field, or sprouted seeds are directly sown. This method is widely practiced in many rice-growing regions.

question: Rice farmers across our delta grow paddy through all three seasons in some years. Does rice cultivation in India vary by season and why can southern states grow rice year-round while northern plains cannot?
context: Rice is primarily cultivated during the Kharif season in the north-western plains zone of India, where it is sown with the onset of the monsoon. However, in the southern and north-eastern parts of the country, rice can be grown in all three seasons including Kharif, Rabi, and Zaid, because these regions experience milder winters and do not have extremely cold weather conditions that would hinder rice cultivation.

question: An agricultural university professor explained that rice follows a C3 photosynthesis pathway. What does this mean for paddy farmers in terms of how the crop performs under different growing conditions?
context: Rice is classified as a C3 plant, meaning it follows the C3 photosynthetic pathway for carbon fixation during photosynthesis. This type of plant generally performs well in environments with adequate water supply and moderate temperatures, which aligns with the typical growing conditions required for rice cultivation.

question: Farmers in four different types of rice growing environments in our state need advice suited to each condition. What are the four major rice farming ecosystems found across India?
context: Rice cultivation in India occurs in four major types of ecosystems. These include irrigated rice ecosystems where crops receive controlled water supply through irrigation systems; rainfed upland rice ecosystems where crops depend mainly on rainfall and are grown on higher land with good drainage; rainfed lowland rice ecosystems where fields retain rainwater naturally; and flood-prone rice ecosystems where crops must tolerate periodic flooding conditions.

question: Rice production statistics shared at a district level meeting showed that rice feeds more than half the world's population. What share of daily calories do rice-eating populations in Asian countries get from this one crop?
context: Rice provides about 29.4 percent of the total daily calories consumed per capita in many Asian countries, making it one of the most important sources of dietary energy.

question: Our rice mill operator says milled rice is less nutritious than raw rice. What protein and fat content is found in milled rice and what happens to nutrients during milling?
context: Milled rice generally contains about 6 to 7 percent protein and a small amount of fat. The fat content is relatively low, around 2.0 to 2.5 percent, and much of this fat is lost during the milling process.

question: Pest management trainers at our KVK explained that rice pest damage varies by region. What are the key principles of managing pests in rice cultivation without causing excessive environmental harm?
context: Pest management in rice cultivation focuses on reducing crop damage caused by insects and other pests that affect plant growth and grain production. Although many rice pests are distributed across India, only a few cause significant economic losses in specific regions. Effective pest management emphasizes the use of good agronomic practices, resistant crop varieties, and the careful use of selective pesticides to control pest populations while minimizing environmental damage.

question: Paddy seed treatment is often skipped by farmers in our village which leads to early seedling diseases. How should paddy seeds be treated before sowing and nursery raising to prevent disease?
context: Disease management in rice cultivation begins with the use of healthy and disease-free seeds, which helps prevent the spread of infections in the field. To protect seeds from fungal and bacterial diseases, they are commonly treated with fungicides such as bavistin at a rate of about 2 grams per kilogram of seed before sowing. In addition to seed treatment, fungicides may also be sprayed in the field when disease symptoms appear in order to control the spread of plant diseases and minimize crop losses.

question: Wheat extension officers in our block say wheat can be grown from near sea level to 3500 meters altitude. What altitude range can wheat be cultivated in and what latitudes does it span globally?
context: Wheat can be cultivated over a wide range of latitudes between 60 degree North and 60 degree South and at altitudes from sea level up to about 3500 meters above mean sea level in tropical and subtropical regions. The crop grows best under cool and moist weather conditions during the vegetative growth stage, followed by warm and dry conditions during grain formation and maturation. The optimum temperature for wheat seed germination is around 20-22 degrees C, although seeds can germinate even at temperatures as low as 4 degrees C.

question: Wheat farmers in our hilly district grow both bread wheat and pasta wheat. What are the two main species of cultivated wheat and how do they differ in use?
context: Two major cultivated species of wheat are widely grown in agriculture. The first is common wheat or bread wheat (Triticum aestivum), which is a hexaploid species and the most widely cultivated wheat in the world. The second is durum wheat (Triticum durum), a tetraploid species that is the second most widely cultivated type of wheat and is commonly used for products such as pasta and semolina.

question: Wheat farmers in our rainfed block want to know if their area gets enough rain for wheat and what type of soil is needed for successful wheat cultivation.
context: Wheat grows well in regions receiving annual rainfall between about 250 mm and 1800 mm. However, the crop cannot tolerate long periods of soil moisture stress. In rainfed conditions, wheat requires evenly distributed winter rainfall of about 15-20 cm to support proper growth. Wheat is adaptable and can be grown on a wide variety of soil types, provided the soils have good drainage and adequate fertility.

question: Wheat farmers in our cooperative add FYM before sowing and wonder if it really helps when chemical fertilizers are also applied. Does applying farmyard manure alongside chemical fertilizers benefit the wheat crop?
context: Organic manures such as farmyard manure (FYM) play an important role in maintaining soil fertility and improving soil structure in wheat cultivation. Application of FYM or other organic manures at about 10 tonnes per hectare during sowing helps enhance soil organic matter, improves nutrient availability, and supports long-term soil productivity.

question: Many wheat growers in our district are also growing rust-susceptible old varieties from years back. What are the three types of rust disease in wheat and which fungicide is most effective for yellow rust control?
context: Wheat crops are commonly affected by three types of rust diseases: brown rust (leaf rust), yellow rust (stripe rust), and black rust (stem rust). These diseases are caused by fungal pathogens belonging to the genus Puccinia. Effective management practices include treating seeds with Trichoderma viride at 4 g per kilogram of seed, avoiding late sowing, maintaining balanced fertilization, and spraying the crop with propiconazole (Tilt 25 EC) at 0.1% when yellow rust first appears. Additional sprays may be repeated at intervals of 10-15 days if necessary.

question: Wild oats are a major problem in wheat fields in our cooperative and chemical methods are needed. What are the effective pre-emergence and post-emergence herbicide options for weed control in wheat fields?
context: The critical period of weed competition in wheat occurs between 30 and 45 days after sowing. Chemical weed control includes pre-emergence application of pendimethalin at about 1 kg active ingredient per hectare within three days after sowing. Post-emergence herbicides such as sulfosulfuron at 25 g per hectare or fenoxaprop-p-ethyl at 100-120 g per hectare may also be applied around 25-30 days after sowing for effective weed control.

question: Maize is the third most important cereal in India after rice and wheat. How much area is under maize cultivation in India and which states lead in maize production?
context: In India, maize is the third most important food crop after rice and wheat. According to data from 2011-12, maize is cultivated on about 8.78 million hectares of land. Most maize cultivation occurs during the Kharif season, which accounts for about 80 percent of the total maize-growing area in the country. The major maize-producing states include Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Himachal Pradesh. Together these states contribute more than 80 percent of the total maize production in India.

question: Maize growers in our cooperative started using raised bed planting but some are still using zero tillage. What are the soil and water management benefits of these two modern maize cultivation methods?
context: For maize cultivation, raised bed planting is considered one of the best crop establishment methods, especially during the monsoon and winter seasons. This method helps manage excess moisture while also improving water use efficiency under rainfed conditions. In addition, maize can also be successfully cultivated under no-till farming systems without primary tillage. No-till maize cultivation helps reduce the cost of cultivation, increase farm profitability, and improve overall resource use efficiency.

question: Maize nutrient management is confusing for many farmers in our block because they do not know when to split nitrogen applications. How much fertilizer and FYM is recommended for maize and when should nitrogen be split?
context: The application of 10-15 tonnes of farmyard manure (FYM) per hectare along with chemical fertilizers is recommended. The recommended fertilizer dose includes 120-150 kg nitrogen (N), 60-80 kg phosphorus (P2O5), 60-70 kg potassium (K2O), and about 25 kg zinc sulphate (ZnSO4) per hectare for high yielding varieties and hybrid maize. During fertilizer application, the full dose of phosphorus and potassium and half of the nitrogen should be applied at the time of sowing. The remaining nitrogen is applied later in two equal splits, one at the knee-high stage and the other at the tasseling stage.

question: Soil type is very important for maize cultivation. What soil conditions are best for growing maize and what soil problems should farmers in waterlogged areas be especially careful about?
context: Maize can grow successfully in a wide variety of soil types, making it a highly adaptable crop. It performs well in soils with a pH range of about 5.0 to 8.0 and can be cultivated in soils ranging from loamy sand to clay loam. However, maize is sensitive to excess soil moisture and waterlogging, therefore soils with good drainage systems are essential to ensure healthy crop growth and prevent root damage.

question: Chickpea farmers in our village want to understand better what crop rotation options they have and how mixing chickpea with other rabi crops benefits the system overall.
context: Chickpea is commonly grown in mixed or rotational cropping systems with other crops. It is often grown mixed with wheat, barley, rapeseed, mustard, and toria in certain regions such as the tarai area. Chickpea is frequently cultivated after harvesting Kharif crops like paddy, maize, sorghum, or pearl millet. Some common crop rotations include paddy-gram, pearl millet-gram, sorghum-gram, maize-gram, and Kharif fallow-gram. These rotations also help control soil-borne diseases.

question: Chickpea farmers in our block often prepare heavily tilled fine seedbed thinking it is better but the extension officer says rougher seedbed is actually needed. What kind of seedbed preparation is recommended for chickpea?
context: Chickpea requires a rough and cloddy seedbed that allows proper aeration in the root zone. Therefore, only limited land preparation is usually needed. The recommended practice is deep ploughing followed by two harrowings to prepare the field. In regions where chickpea is grown using residual soil moisture, such as in the Haveli system of Madhya Pradesh, deep summer ploughing helps improve moisture retention in the soil.

question: Chickpea farmers in our FPO want to know how much moisture the crop needs and whether they should irrigate or if residual moisture is enough throughout the season.
context: Chickpea is mostly grown as a rainfed crop and can extract moisture from deep soil layers, sometimes more than one meter deep. However, where irrigation facilities are available, a pre-sowing irrigation known as palewa is recommended. If winter rains are insufficient, irrigation should be applied at critical stages such as pre-flowering and pod development. The crop generally requires about 250-400 mm of water during its growth period.

question: A farmer in our village tried nipping chickpea on one plot and skipped it on another. The nipped plot gave more pods per plant. What is the scientific reason why nipping increases yield in chickpea?
context: Nipping is an important cultural practice in irrigated chickpea cultivation. It involves removing the apical buds or top auxiliary buds of the plant when the crop reaches a height of about 15-20 cm, usually around 50 days after sowing. This process stops excessive vertical growth and encourages the development of lateral branches, making the plants more vigorous and increasing the number of flowers and pods produced.

question: Weed control in chickpea fields in our cooperative is mainly done by hand but labor is now very expensive. What chemical weed control methods can be used in chickpea fields effectively?
context: Weeds can cause severe yield losses in chickpea fields, especially during the first four to eight weeks after sowing, which is considered the critical period of weed competition. Chemical weed control using pendimethalin as a pre-emergence herbicide at about 1.0 kg active ingredient per hectare followed by hoeing at 45 days after sowing has also been found effective. Intercropping chickpea with mustard can also reduce weed infestation.

question: Pigeonpea farmers in our cooperative want to know what soil and climate conditions are ideally suited for high-yielding arhar cultivation in their region.
context: Pigeonpea is mainly grown in arid and semi-arid climates between 30 degrees N and 35 degrees S latitudes. It thrives well in areas receiving about 500-1000 mm annual rainfall and is well suited to low rainfall regions because of its deep taproot system that provides drought tolerance. The crop grows best at temperatures ranging from 20 degrees C to 40 degrees C. Sandy loam to loam soils rich in organic matter are ideal for pigeonpea cultivation. The soil should be deep, well-drained, and free from soluble salts. The crop can grow in soils with pH ranging from 5.5 to 8.0, although the most favorable pH is between 6.0 and 6.5.

question: Arhar farmers in our block want to know what improved varieties are available and which ones are suitable for a wheat-based rotation system where early maturity is important.
context: Several improved pigeonpea cultivars have been developed for better yield and disease resistance. Some important varieties include Pusa 855, Pusa 991, Pusa 992, Pusa 2001, Pusa 2002, UPAS 120, Manak, AL-15, and AL 201. For pigeonpea-wheat crop rotation systems, varieties such as Pusa 991, Pusa 992, Pusa 2001, and Pusa 2002 are considered suitable.

question: Pigeonpea farmers in our cooperative want to know how much seed per hectare and what spacing to use for medium and long duration varieties on their rainfed black cotton soil farms.
context: The seed rate in pigeonpea depends on the maturity duration of the variety. Long duration varieties require about 8-10 kg seed per hectare, medium duration varieties require about 10-12 kg per hectare, and short duration varieties require about 12-15 kg per hectare. Seeds are usually sown at a depth of about 4-6 cm in moist soil. For short duration varieties, a row spacing of 40-60 cm with plant spacing of 10-15 cm is recommended, while long duration varieties require wider spacing of 60-120 cm between rows and 10-20 cm between plants.

question: Arhar farmers in our cooperative say they get better yields with irrigation during flower and pod fill stages than depending on rainfall alone. How much water does pigeonpea need and when is irrigation most critical?
context: Pigeonpea generally requires about 35-40 cm of water throughout its growth period. The crop usually does not require irrigation when grown in areas with assured rainfall. However, moisture is particularly important during budding, flowering, and pod formation stages. If drought conditions occur, protective irrigation may be applied in alternate rows. The use of crop residues or biomass from intercrops as mulch helps conserve soil moisture and maintain soil microbial activity.

question: Weed management in pigeonpea is neglected by many farmers in our village because the crop shades weeds later. But early weeds cause serious damage. When should weeding be done in pigeonpea and is there a chemical option?
context: Weed control in pigeonpea is mainly required during the first 60 days after sowing when weeds compete with the crop for nutrients and moisture. The first weeding is generally done about 20-25 days after sowing, followed by a second hoeing around 50-60 days after sowing. Pre-emergence application of pendimethalin at about 1.0 kg active ingredient per hectare is also effective in controlling weeds.

question: Field pea farmers in UP and MP grow two main types of peas. What is field pea as a pulse crop, how nutritious is it, and how much is grown in India?
context: Pea (Pisum sativum L.) is an important pulse crop cultivated in India for both food and nutritional purposes. Field pea is mainly grown for dry seeds which are used in the preparation of dal and various snack foods. Pea seeds are highly nutritious, containing about 22.5 percent protein, 62.1 percent carbohydrates, 1.8 percent fats, and important minerals such as calcium and iron along with vitamins like riboflavin and thiamin. In India, field pea is grown on about 0.62 million hectares with an annual production of about 0.56 million tonnes and an average productivity of around 906 kg per hectare.

question: Field pea farmers in our UP cooperative want to know which improved varieties are available and which ones perform well in their region.
context: Several improved varieties of field pea have been developed for cultivation in different parts of India. Some prominent varieties include Pant P 5, DMR 11, VL-1, T 163, Rachna, PG 3, and Pusa Prabhat. These varieties are selected for better yield potential and improved adaptability to different agro-climatic conditions.

question: Pea growers in our cooperative want to plan their crop rotation better. Which crops are commonly grown with or after field peas in different farming systems across India?
context: Peas are often grown in mixed cropping or rotational systems with other crops. They are commonly grown with wheat, barley, oats, rapeseed, and mustard. Pea is also used as an intercrop in autumn sugarcane. Some common crop rotations involving peas include paddy-pea, maize-pea, sorghum-pea, pearl millet-pea, cotton-pea, maize-early pea-sugarcane, and maize-pea-okra cropping systems.

question: Field pea farmers in our district want to know what soil and temperature conditions are needed for peas to germinate and grow well without suffering from heat stress.
context: Peas grow best in cool climatic conditions with moderate temperatures and relatively high humidity. Most pea cultivars can tolerate light frost, but temperatures above about 27 degrees C can negatively affect crop growth and yield. The crop is particularly sensitive to moisture stress during the flowering stage. High humidity combined with cloudy weather can also promote the spread of fungal diseases such as damping-off and powdery mildew. Peas require well-drained sandy loam or sandy clay loam soils with a pH range of about 6.5 to 7.5.

question: Field pea growers in our cooperative want to know what seed treatment, seed rate, and sowing time to follow for the best crop establishment in northern India.
context: The optimum time for sowing field pea in northern India is during the second fortnight of October. The seed rate generally ranges from about 60 to 80 kg per hectare depending on the seed size, variety, and sowing method. Before sowing, seeds should be treated with thiram at about 0.25 percent to protect against diseases. For proper nitrogen fixation and good nodulation, seeds are also treated with Rhizobium leguminosarum culture. Field peas are typically sown in rows spaced about 30-45 cm apart.

question: Field pea farmers in our cooperative want to know how much fertilizer to apply since pea is a legume and presumably needs less nitrogen than cereals.
context: Although peas are legume crops capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, they still require a starter dose of nutrients for proper early growth. Generally, about 20 kg nitrogen, 50-60 kg phosphorus (P2O5), and 30-40 kg potassium (K2O) per hectare are applied at the time of planting to ensure balanced nutrition and good crop development.

question: Pea growers in our dryland cooperative struggle with moisture stress at the flowering stage which causes significant yield loss. When should pea crops be irrigated and which stages are most critical?
context: Drought is a major constraint affecting pea cultivation in India. The crop is usually sown after irrigation to ensure adequate soil moisture for germination. During crop growth, irrigation should be applied carefully using light and uniform watering. The most critical stages for irrigation are the branching stage and the flowering stage, where sufficient soil moisture is essential for achieving good yields.

question: Pea crops in our cooperative fields get heavily infested with weeds in the first month. What weed management approaches are most effective in field pea cultivation?
context: Weeds compete strongly with pea plants during the early growth period, particularly between 30 and 45 days after sowing, which is considered the critical period of weed competition. Effective weed control can be achieved by keeping the field weed-free through two manual weedings and hoeing operations, usually carried out around three and six weeks after germination. In addition, pre-emergence application of pendimethalin at about 1.0 kg active ingredient per hectare can effectively control weeds.

question: Pea plants in several fields in our block showed a white powdery coating on pods and leaves that reduced marketable yield badly. What disease is this and which resistant varieties and fungicides work against it?
context: Powdery mildew is a common fungal disease affecting pea crops. It appears as a white powdery fungal growth consisting of mycelium and spores on leaves, stems, tendrils, petioles, and pods. Infected pods become dull and lose their bright green appearance. Resistant varieties such as Rachna, Pant Matar 5, DMR 7, and HUP 2 can help reduce disease incidence. In susceptible varieties, spraying wettable sulphur 70 WP at about 0.3 percent concentration at intervals of around 10 days can effectively control the disease.

question: Pod borers attack pea crops in our area during the pod formation stage and cause serious economic damage. What insecticide schedule is recommended to control pod borer in peas?
context: Major insect pests affecting pea crops include leaf miners and pea pod borers. These pests damage the leaves and pods, reducing crop productivity. Effective control of pea pod borer can be achieved by spraying monocrotophos at about 0.04 percent concentration at intervals of 10-15 days starting from the pod formation stage.

question: Field pea farmers in our cooperative harvest for both green pod sale and dry grain. What yields can farmers expect and when is the right time to harvest field peas for each purpose?
context: Field pea crops should be harvested when the pods are fully mature and the plants are completely dry. After harvesting, the crop is dried in the sun before threshing to separate the grains. Under improved cultivation practices, peas can produce about 10-12 tonnes of green pods per hectare. When grown for dry grain, field pea yields usually range between about 2-3 tonnes per hectare.

question: Greengram farmers in our cooperative grow the summer crop between wheat and paddy in May-June. What climate and soil conditions does greengram need to grow successfully?
context: Greengram is primarily a tropical crop but can also grow well in subtropical regions. It is cultivated in areas between 30 degrees N and 30 degrees S latitude and can grow from sea level up to an altitude of about 2000 meters. The crop grows well in regions receiving 50-75 cm annual rainfall. It prefers well-drained loamy to sandy loam soils. Greengram does not grow well in saline, alkaline, or waterlogged soils and waterlogging adversely affects the crop.
